claim: Substrate-binding proteins (SBPs) are associated with ATP-binding cassette importers.
source: Substrate-binding proteins (SBPs) are associated with ATP-binding cassette importers and switch from an open to a closed conformation upon substrate binding, providing specificity for transport.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that establishes the relationship between SBPs and ABC importers, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: SBPs switch from an open to a closed conformation upon substrate binding.
source: Substrate-binding proteins (SBPs) are associated with ATP-binding cassette importers and switch from an open to a closed conformation upon substrate binding, providing specificity for transport.
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism described in the abstract and supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SBP conformational switching provides specificity for transport.
source: Substrate-binding proteins (SBPs) are associated with ATP-binding cassette importers and switch from an open to a closed conformation upon substrate binding, providing specificity for transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings throughout the manuscript showing how different conformations relate to transport activity.

claim: Single-molecule FRET reveals an unrecognized diversity of plasticity in SBPs.
source: Using single-molecule FRET, we reveal an unrecognized diversity of plasticity in SBPs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the smFRET experimental data presented in Figures 2-6.

claim: A unique closed SBP conformation does not exist for transported substrates.
source: We show that a unique closed SBP conformation does not exist for transported substrates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the smFRET data showing multiple distinct conformations for different cognate substrates (Figure 2D-F).

claim: SBPs sample a range of conformations that activate transport.
source: Instead, SBPs sample a range of conformations that activate transport.
evidence: This is supported by the FRET data showing multiple conformations for cognate substrates that are all transported (Figure 2).

claim: Certain non-transported ligands leave the SBP structure largely unaltered.
source: Certain non-transported ligands leave the structure largely unaltered or trigger a conformation distinct from that of transported substrates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET data showing that arginine and lysine binding to SBD1 and arginine to SBD2 do not alter FRET efficiency (Figure 4D-E).

claim: Some non-transported ligands trigger a conformation distinct from that of transported substrates.
source: Certain non-transported ligands leave the structure largely unaltered or trigger a conformation distinct from that of transported substrates.
evidence: This is shown by FRET data for non-cognate ligands inducing different conformations than cognate substrates (Figure 4).

claim: In some cases, similar SBP conformations are formed by both transported and non-transported ligands.
source: Intriguingly, in some cases, similar SBP conformations are formed by both transported and non-transported ligands.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PsaA binding both Mn2+ (cognate) and Zn2+ (non-cognate) with similar FRET efficiencies (Figure 4H).

claim: When similar conformations are formed by transported and non-transported ligands, the inability for transport can arise from slow opening of the SBP.
source: In this case, the inability for transport arises from slow opening of the SBP or the selectivity provided by the translocator.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Zn2+-PsaA complex showing extremely slow opening compared to Mn2+-PsaA (Figure 5).

claim: When similar conformations are formed by transported and non-transported ligands, the inability for transport can arise from the selectivity provided by the translocator.
source: In this case, the inability for transport arises from slow opening of the SBP or the selectivity provided by the translocator.
evidence: This is inferred from the MalE data with maltooctaose and maltodecaose showing similar conformations and opening kinetics to maltoheptaose but not being transported (Figure 6).

claim: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters facilitate the unidirectional trans-bilayer movement of a diverse array of molecules using the energy released from ATP hydrolysis.
source: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters facilitate the unidirectional trans-bilayer movement of a diverse array of molecules using the energy released from ATP hydrolysis (Higgins, 1992).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about ABC transporters supported by citation to Higgins, 1992.

claim: ABC transporters share a common architecture with two transmembrane domains (TMDs) that form the translocation pathway and two cytoplasmic nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) which bind and hydrolyze ATP.
source: They share a common architecture, with the translocator unit comprising two transmembrane domains (TMDs) that form the translocation pathway and two cytoplasmic nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) which bind and hydrolyze ATP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC transporter architecture.

claim: ABC importers require an additional extra-cytoplasmic accessory protein referred to as a substrate-binding protein (SBP) or domain (SBD).
source: ABC importers require an additional extra-cytoplasmic accessory protein referred to as a substrate-binding protein (SBP) or domain (SBD; hereafter SBDs and SBPs are both termed SBPs) (Berntsson et al., 2010; Scheepers et al., 2016; van der Heide and Poolman, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: ABC importers that employ SBPs can be subdivided as Type I or Type II based on structural and mechanistic distinctions.
source: ABC importers that employ SBPs can be subdivided as Type I or Type II based on structural and mechanistic distinctions (Locher, 2016; Swier et al., 2016).
evidence: This classification is supported by citations to Locher, 2016 and Swier et al., 2016.

claim: A unifying feature of the transport mechanism of Type I and Type II ABC importers is the binding and delivery of substrate from a dedicated SBP to the translocator unit for import into the cytoplasm.
source: A unifying feature of the transport mechanism of Type I and Type II ABC importers is the binding and delivery of substrate from a dedicated SBP to the translocator unit for import into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a mechanistic principle supported by the literature and the experimental findings in this study.

claim: Bacterial genomes encode multiple distinct ABC importers to facilitate the acquisition of essential nutrients such as sugars, amino acids, vitamins, compatible solutes, and metal ions.
source: Bacterial genomes encode multiple distinct ABC importers to facilitate the acquisition of essential nutrients such as sugars, amino acids, vitamins, compatible solutes, and metal ions (Higgins, 1992; Davidson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Higgins, 1992 and Davidson et al., 2008.

claim: Many ABC importers can transport more than one type of substrate molecule using high-affinity interactions between SBPs and transported ligands.
source: Many ABC importers can transport more than one type of substrate molecule using high-affinity interactions between SBPs and transported ligands (herein termed cognate substrates) (Berntsson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berntsson et al., 2010 and demonstrated by the experimental data in this study.

claim: Despite low-sequence similarity between SBPs of different ABC importers, they share a common architecture comprising two structurally conserved rigid lobes connected by a flexible hinge region.
source: Despite low-sequence similarity between SBPs of different ABC importers, they share a common architecture comprising two structurally conserved rigid lobes connected by a flexible hinge region (Figure 1) (Berntsson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berntsson et al., 2010 and illustrated in Figure 1 showing crystal structures.

claim: Biophysical and structural analyses indicate that ligand binding at the interface of the two lobes facilitates switching between an open and a closed conformation.
source: Numerous biophysical (Shilton et al., 1996) and structural analyses (Quiocho and Ledvina, 1996) indicate that ligand binding at the interface of the two lobes facilitates switching between two conformations, that is from an open to a closed conformation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shilton et al., 1996 and Quiocho and Ledvina, 1996.

claim: Bending and unbending of the hinge region brings the two lobes together (closed conformation) or apart (open conformation), respectively.
source: Bending and unbending of the hinge region brings the two lobes together (closed conformation) or apart (open conformation), respectively.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of SBP conformational changes based on structural knowledge.

claim: Crystallographic analyses show that the amount of opening varies between different SBPs.
source: Crystallographic analyses show that the amount of opening varies between different SBPs; the lobe-movements observed range from small rearrangements as in the Type II SBP BtuF (Karpowich et al., 2003), to complete reorientation of both lobes by angles as large as 60° in the Type I SBP LivJ (Trakhanov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystallographic studies (Karpowich et al., 2003; Trakhanov et al., 2005).

claim: The lobe-movements observed in SBPs range from small rearrangements as in the Type II SBP BtuF to complete reorientation of both lobes by angles as large as 60° in the Type I SBP LivJ.
source: Crystallographic analyses show that the amount of opening varies between different SBPs; the lobe-movements observed range from small rearrangements as in the Type II SBP BtuF (Karpowich et al., 2003), to complete reorientation of both lobes by angles as large as 60° in the Type I SBP LivJ (Trakhanov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific crystallographic studies.

claim: The hinge region is the most defining feature of each sub-group or cluster in the structural classification of SBPs.
source: Nevertheless, the wealth of structural data permits a structural classification of SBPs, wherein the hinge region is the most defining feature of each sub-group or cluster (Figure 1) (Berntsson et al., 2010; Scheepers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berntsson et al., 2010 and Scheepers et al., 2016, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Crystal structures of the same protein with different ligands bound generally report the same degree of closing of the SBP.
source: Crystal structures of the same protein, but with different ligands bound, generally report the same degree of closing of the SBP (Trakhanov et al., 2005; Nishitani et al., 2012; Pandey et al., 2016; Magnusson et al., 2004; Quiocho et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to crystallographic studies.

claim: It is assumed that the conformational switching of the SBPs enables the ABC transporter to allosterically sense the loading state of the SBP-ligand complex ('translocation competency'), thereby contributing to transport specificity.
source: Thus, it is assumed that the conformational switching of the SBPs enables the ABC transporter to allosterically sense the loading state of the SBP-ligand complex ('translocation competency'), thereby contributing to transport specificity (Davidson et al., 2008; Quiocho and Ledvina, 1996).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations to Davidson et al., 2008 and Quiocho and Ledvina, 1996.

claim: Crystal structures of the SBP MalE show that the protein adopts a unique closed conformation when interacting with cognate ligands maltose, maltotriose and maltotetraose.
source: For example, crystal structures of the SBP MalE show that the protein adopts a unique closed conformation when interacting with cognate ligands maltose, maltotriose and maltotetraose (Quiocho et al., 1997), while the non-transported ligand β-cyclodextrin is bound by MalE (Hall et al., 1997a) but fails to trigger formation of the closed conformation (Hall et al., 1997b; Sharff et al., 1993; Skrynnikov et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Quiocho et al., 1997.

claim: The non-transported ligand β-cyclodextrin is bound by MalE but fails to trigger formation of the closed conformation.
source: For example, crystal structures of the SBP MalE show that the protein adopts a unique closed conformation when interacting with cognate ligands maltose, maltotriose and maltotetraose (Quiocho et al., 1997), while the non-transported ligand β-cyclodextrin is bound by MalE (Hall et al., 1997a) but fails to trigger formation of the closed conformation (Hall et al., 1997b; Sharff et al., 1993; Skrynnikov et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall et al., 1997a, Hall et al., 1997b, Sharff et al., 1993, and Skrynnikov et al., 2000.

claim: Only SBPs which adopt the closed conformation can productively interact with the translocator and initiate transport.
source: Such findings suggest that only SBPs which adopt the closed conformation can productively interact with the translocator and initiate transport.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the MalE-β-cyclodextrin example, but the manuscript challenges this assumption.

claim: The TMDs of certain ABC importers interact directly with their substrates.
source: However, the TMDs of certain ABC importers were also shown to interact directly with their substrates.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to MalFGK2E and Art(QM)2 studies.

claim: In MalFGK2E from Escherichia coli, substrate-binding pockets have been identified inside the TMDs.
source: In MalFGK2E (Oldham et al., 2013) from Escherichia coli and Art(QM)2 (Yu et al., 2015) from Thermoanaerobacter tengcongensi substrate-binding pockets have been identified inside the TMDs, and these might be linked to regulation of transport.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oldham et al., 2013.

claim: In Art(QM)2 from Thermoanaerobacter tengcongensi, substrate-binding pockets have been identified inside the TMDs.
source: In MalFGK2E (Oldham et al., 2013) from Escherichia coli and Art(QM)2 (Yu et al., 2015) from Thermoanaerobacter tengcongensi substrate-binding pockets have been identified inside the TMDs, and these might be linked to regulation of transport.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2015.

claim: Substrate-binding pockets inside the TMDs might be linked to regulation of transport.
source: In MalFGK2E (Oldham et al., 2013) from Escherichia coli and Art(QM)2 (Yu et al., 2015) from Thermoanaerobacter tengcongensi substrate-binding pockets have been identified inside the TMDs, and these might be linked to regulation of transport.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of TMD binding pockets.

claim: Similar binding pockets within the TMDs have not been observed in the high-resolution structures of other ABC importers.
source: Similar binding pockets within the TMDs have not been observed in the high-resolution structures of other ABC importers, although cavities through which the substrate passes in the transition of the TMD from outward- to inward-facing are likely to be present in all the transporters (Woo et al., 2012; Pinkett et al., 2007; Locher et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies (Woo et al., 2012; Pinkett et al., 2007; Locher et al., 2002).

claim: Cavities through which the substrate passes in the transition of the TMD from outward- to inward-facing are likely to be present in all ABC transporters.
source: Similar binding pockets within the TMDs have not been observed in the high-resolution structures of other ABC importers, although cavities through which the substrate passes in the transition of the TMD from outward- to inward-facing are likely to be present in all the transporters (Woo et al., 2012; Pinkett et al., 2007; Locher et al., 2002).
evidence: This is inferred from structural studies cited (Woo et al., 2012; Pinkett et al., 2007; Locher et al., 2002).

claim: Crystallographic, NMR, and single-molecule studies indicate that SBPs can undergo intrinsic conformational changes in the absence of substrate.
source: Additional complexity exists for the coupling of SBP conformational switching and the ligand recognition process, as crystallographic (Flocco and Mowbray, 1994; Oswald et al., 2008), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) (Tang et al., 2007) and single-molecule (Feng et al., 2016; Gouridis et al., 2015) studies indicate that SBPs can undergo intrinsic conformational changes in the absence of substrate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple types of studies.

claim: Crystal structures of the SBPs MalE and a D-xylose SBP were obtained in an open ligand-bound conformation.
source: Furthermore, crystal structures of the SBPs MalE and a D-xylose SBP were obtained in an open ligand-bound conformation (Duan and Quiocho, 2002; Sooriyaarachchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duan and Quiocho, 2002 and Sooriyaarachchi et al., 2010.

claim: Six distinct SBPs were selected for study: PsaA (cluster A), MalE (cluster B), OppA (cluster C), SBD1 and SBD2 of GlnPQ, and OpuAC (all cluster F).
source: Six distinct SBPs were selected (Figure 1) (Fulyani et al., 2016; Wolters et al., 2010; Ferenci, 1980; McDevitt et al., 2011; Berntsson et al., 2011), based on two criteria. First, they cover the breadth of SBP structural classes: PsaA (cluster A), MalE (cluster B), OppA (cluster C), SBD1 and SBD2 of GlnPQ, and OpuAC (all cluster F).
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The selected SBPs provide coverage of hinge region diversity.
source: The selected SBPs provide coverage of hinge region diversity (Berntsson et al., 2010; Scheepers et al., 2016), thereby addressing a hypothesized key determinant in SBP conformational dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berntsson et al., 2010 and Scheepers et al., 2016.

claim: The hinge region is a hypothesized key determinant in SBP conformational dynamics.
source: The selected SBPs provide coverage of hinge region diversity (Berntsson et al., 2010; Scheepers et al., 2016), thereby addressing a hypothesized key determinant in SBP conformational dynamics.
evidence: This is a hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: The selected SBPs belong to Type I and Type II ABC importers with extensively characterized substrate interactions.
source: Second, the selected SBPs belong to Type I and Type II ABC importers with extensively characterized substrate (cognate and non-cognate) interactions, such as metal ions (PsaA) (McDevitt et al., 2011), sugars (MalE) (Ferenci et al., 1986), peptides (OppA) (Doeven et al., 2004), amino acids (SBD1 and SBD2) (Fulyani et al., 2016), and compatible solutes (OpuAC) (Wolters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing each SBP.

claim: PsaA binds metal ions.
source: Second, the selected SBPs belong to Type I and Type II ABC importers with extensively characterized substrate (cognate and non-cognate) interactions, such as metal ions (PsaA) (McDevitt et al., 2011), sugars (MalE) (Ferenci et al., 1986), peptides (OppA) (Doeven et al., 2004), amino acids (SBD1 and SBD2) (Fulyani et al., 2016), and compatible solutes (OpuAC) (Wolters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McDevitt et al., 2011.

claim: MalE binds sugars.
source: Second, the selected SBPs belong to Type I and Type II ABC importers with extensively characterized substrate (cognate and non-cognate) interactions, such as metal ions (PsaA) (McDevitt et al., 2011), sugars (MalE) (Ferenci et al., 1986), peptides (OppA) (Doeven et al., 2004), amino acids (SBD1 and SBD2) (Fulyani et al., 2016), and compatible solutes (OpuAC) (Wolters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ferenci et al., 1986.

claim: OppA binds peptides.
source: Second, the selected SBPs belong to Type I and Type II ABC importers with extensively characterized substrate (cognate and non-cognate) interactions, such as metal ions (PsaA) (McDevitt et al., 2011), sugars (MalE) (Ferenci et al., 1986), peptides (OppA) (Doeven et al., 2004), amino acids (SBD1 and SBD2) (Fulyani et al., 2016), and compatible solutes (OpuAC) (Wolters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Doeven et al., 2004.

claim: SBD1 and SBD2 bind amino acids.
source: Second, the selected SBPs belong to Type I and Type II ABC importers with extensively characterized substrate (cognate and non-cognate) interactions, such as metal ions (PsaA) (McDevitt et al., 2011), sugars (MalE) (Ferenci et al., 1986), peptides (OppA) (Doeven et al., 2004), amino acids (SBD1 and SBD2) (Fulyani et al., 2016), and compatible solutes (OpuAC) (Wolters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fulyani et al., 2016.

claim: OpuAC binds compatible solutes.
source: Second, the selected SBPs belong to Type I and Type II ABC importers with extensively characterized substrate (cognate and non-cognate) interactions, such as metal ions (PsaA) (McDevitt et al., 2011), sugars (MalE) (Ferenci et al., 1986), peptides (OppA) (Doeven et al., 2004), amino acids (SBD1 and SBD2) (Fulyani et al., 2016), and compatible solutes (OpuAC) (Wolters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wolters et al., 2010.

claim: Labeling and surface-immobilization of the protein molecules did not alter the ligand dissociation constant KD.
source: Labeling and surface-immobilization of the protein molecules did not alter the ligand dissociation constant KD (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the KD values in Table 1 comparing labeled and unlabeled proteins.

claim: Steady-state anisotropy measurements indicate that the dyes retain sufficient rotational freedom.
source: Steady-state anisotropy measurements indicate that the dyes retain sufficient rotational freedom (Table 2) so that relative inter-dye distance can be assessed via the apparent FRET efficiency of freely diffusing or surface-immobilized protein molecules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the anisotropy data in Table 2.

claim: Saturating concentrations of cognate substrate shift the FRET efficiency histograms to higher values compared to the ligand-free SBPs.
source: Saturating concentrations of cognate substrate, above the KD (Table 1), shift the FRET efficiency histograms and the fitted Gaussian distributions to higher values compared to the ligand-free SBPs (Figure 2B–G; Supplementary file 3), indicating a reduced distance between the SBP lobes and inferred to be closure of the proteins.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B-G and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Higher FRET efficiency indicates a reduced distance between the SBP lobes and closure of the proteins.
source: Saturating concentrations of cognate substrate, above the KD (Table 1), shift the FRET efficiency histograms and the fitted Gaussian distributions to higher values compared to the ligand-free SBPs (Figure 2B–G; Supplementary file 3), indicating a reduced distance between the SBP lobes and inferred to be closure of the proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET principle and the data in Figure 2.

claim: Ligand-induced opening and closing transitions were observed in individual surface-immobilized SBPs in the presence of ligand concentrations at the respective KD value.
source: For individual surface-immobilized SBPs, we observed ligand-induced opening and closing transitions in the presence of ligand concentrations at the respective KD value (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The solution-based FRET distributions of ligand-bound and ligand-free SBPs are unimodal and do not reveal substantial conformational heterogeneity.
source: The solution-based FRET distributions of ligand-bound and ligand-free SBPs are unimodal and thus do not reveal any substantial conformational heterogeneity, such as a pronounced closing in the absence of substrate or a substantial population of an open-liganded state (vide infra).
evidence: This is observed in the FRET histograms in Figure 2.

claim: Ligands are bound via an induced-fit mechanism.
source: This strongly suggests that ligands are bound via an induced-fit mechanism, unless dynamics occur on timescales faster than milliseconds.
evidence: This is inferred from the unimodal FRET distributions and the absence of substantial open-liganded states.

claim: Substrate-induced SBP closing follows first-order kinetics for OppA.
source: This inference was confirmed for OppA by examining individual surface-immobilized proteins and demonstrating that substrate-induced SBP closing follows first-order kinetics while the opening obeys zeroth-order kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013.

claim: The opening of OppA obeys zeroth-order kinetics.
source: This inference was confirmed for OppA by examining individual surface-immobilized proteins and demonstrating that substrate-induced SBP closing follows first-order kinetics while the opening obeys zeroth-order kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013.

claim: Multiple substrate-bound SBP conformations exist for SBD1, SBD2 and MalE.
source: Further examination of the FRET distributions shows that multiple substrate-bound SBP conformations exist for SBD1, SBD2 and MalE (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Asparagine and glutamine stabilize distinct conformations in SBD1.
source: For the amino acid binding-proteins SBD1 and SBD2, the cognate substrates (Fulyani et al., 2016) asparagine and glutamine for SBD1, and glutamine and glutamate for SBD2 all stabilize a distinct protein conformation, as shown by the FRET efficiency histograms and fitted Gaussian distributions (Figure 2E–F; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Glutamine and glutamate stabilize distinct conformations in SBD2.
source: For the amino acid binding-proteins SBD1 and SBD2, the cognate substrates (Fulyani et al., 2016) asparagine and glutamine for SBD1, and glutamine and glutamate for SBD2 all stabilize a distinct protein conformation, as shown by the FRET efficiency histograms and fitted Gaussian distributions (Figure 2E–F; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Asparagine binding reduces the inter-dye distance in SBD1 by ~9 Å.
source: Notably, closure of SBD1 by asparagine reduces the inter-dye distance compared to the ligand-free protein by ~9 Å (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Glutamine binding reduces the inter-dye distance in SBD1 by ~5 Å, suggesting only partial closing.
source: In contrast, glutamine binding reduces the distance by ~5 Å, suggesting that only a partial closing of SBD1 occurs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Glutamine binding reduces the inter-dye distance in SBD2 by ~9 Å.
source: In SBD2, glutamine and glutamate reduce the distance ~9 and ~7 Å, respectively (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Glutamate binding reduces the inter-dye distance in SBD2 by ~7 Å.
source: In SBD2, glutamine and glutamate reduce the distance ~9 and ~7 Å, respectively (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: At least three distinct ligand-bound MalE conformations exist.
source: Comparison of the FRET efficiency histograms of the different MalE-ligand complexes shows that at least three distinct ligand-bound MalE conformations exist (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Some cognate substrates did not induce a unique MalE conformation.
source: In contrast to SBD1 and SBD2, some cognate substrates did not induce a unique MalE conformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Maltopentaose and maltohexaose elicit the same FRET change in MalE.
source: For example, maltopentaose and maltohexaose elicited the same FRET change, and triggered the formation of a partially closed MalE conformation with a ~7 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Maltopentaose and maltohexaose trigger formation of a partially closed MalE conformation with a ~7 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
source: For example, maltopentaose and maltohexaose elicited the same FRET change, and triggered the formation of a partially closed MalE conformation with a ~7 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Maltose, maltotriose and maltotetraose induce a fully closed form of MalE with a ~10 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
source: This conformational state is different from the fully closed form of MalE, induced by maltose, maltotriose and maltotetraose, wherein the inter-dye distance is reduced by ~10 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Maltoheptaose induces a partially closed MalE conformation with a ~5 Å reduction in the inter-dye distance.
source: Further, it is also distinct from the other partially closed conformation induced by maltoheptaose where the inter-dye distance is reduced by ~5 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The four examined cognate substrates of OppA elicit the same FRET change.
source: However, whether this conformational plasticity is a universal feature among SBPs needs to be investigated further, because in OppA the four examined cognate substrates (Doeven et al., 2004) elicited the same FRET change (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The findings on conformational changes for each SBP were shown to be statistically robust by the non-parametric two-way Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test.
source: The findings on the conformational changes (and differences) for each SBP were shown to be statistically robust by the non-parametric two-way Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test (p-values in Supplementary file 1), which indicates the absence of any fitting bias.
evidence: This is stated in the text with p-values provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Although the examined SBPs have a single open conformation, a productive interaction between the SBP and the translocator does not require a single, unique closed SBP conformation.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that although the examined SBPs have a single open conformation, a productive interaction between the SBP and the translocator does not require a single, unique closed SBP conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRET data showing multiple conformations that support transport.

claim: The structural flexibility of the SBP permits the formation of one or more ligand-bound conformations, all of which are able to interact with the translocator and initiate transport.
source: The structural flexibility of the SBP permits the formation of one or more ligand-bound conformations, all of which are able to interact with the translocator and initiate transport (Fulyani et al., 2016; Wolters et al., 2010; Ferenci, 1980; McDevitt et al., 2011; Doeven et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the FRET data and citations to transport studies.

claim: In ligand-free MalE, PsaA and OpuAC, no transitions to higher FRET states were observed within a total observation time of >8 min for each SBP.
source: For ligand-free MalE, PsaA and OpuAC, no transitions to higher FRET states were observed within a total observation time of >8 min for each SBP (Figure 3B–D; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B-D and Supplementary file 4.

claim: In SBD1, SBD2 and OppA, rare transitions to a high FRET state can be observed.
source: In SBD1, SBD2 and OppA rare transitions to a high FRET state can be observed and have an average lifetime of 205 ± 36, 90 ± 11 and 211 ± 42 ms (mean ± s.e.m.), respectively (Figure 3E–G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: The average lifetime of the high FRET state in ligand-free SBD1 is 205 ± 36 ms.
source: In SBD1, SBD2 and OppA rare transitions to a high FRET state can be observed and have an average lifetime of 205 ± 36, 90 ± 11 and 211 ± 42 ms (mean ± s.e.m.), respectively (Figure 3E–G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claim: The average lifetime of the high FRET state in ligand-free SBD2 is 90 ± 11 ms.
source: In SBD1, SBD2 and OppA rare transitions to a high FRET state can be observed and have an average lifetime of 205 ± 36, 90 ± 11 and 211 ± 42 ms (mean ± s.e.m.), respectively (Figure 3E–G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claim: Maltose, maltotriose and maltotetraose induce similar MalE conformations.
source: These steps most likely occur after opening of MalE, as these differences in transport activity are unlikely to arise from differences in docking of MalE onto the TMDs (crystallographic (Quiocho et al., 1997) and smFRET data (Supplementary file 3) shows that maltose, maltotriose and maltotetraose induce similar MalE conformations) or the differences in the binding affinity of MalE (Hall et al., 1997a).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data (Quiocho et al., 1997) and smFRET data (Supplementary file 3).

claim: The positive correlation between lifetime of the SBP closed conformation and the activity of the transporter strongly suggests involvement of the translocator MalFGK2 in influencing the transport rate of certain maltodextrins.
source: Thus, although the precise molecular mechanism of the rate-determining steps remains elusive, the positive correlation between lifetime of the SBP closed conformation and the activity of the transporter strongly suggests involvement of the translocator MalFGK2 in influencing the transport rate of certain maltodextrins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: The general view of SBP conformational changes serving as a binary switch to communicate transport competency may hold for some SBPs, such as OppA.
source: The general view of SBP conformational changes serving as a binary switch to communicate transport competency may hold for some SBPs, such as OppA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), while others employ multiple distinct ligand-bound conformations (Figure 2D–F; Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that OppA shows a single conformation for all cognate substrates.

claim: Some SBPs employ multiple distinct ligand-bound conformations.
source: The general view of SBP conformational changes serving as a binary switch to communicate transport competency may hold for some SBPs, such as OppA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), while others employ multiple distinct ligand-bound conformations (Figure 2D–F; Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D-F and Figure 4D-G.

claim: MalE shows a remarkable structural flexibility of at least six different ligand-bound conformations.
source: MalE shows a remarkable structural flexibility of at least six different ligand-bound conformations (Figure 2D; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 4F.

claim: SBD1 can sample at least four distinct ligand-bound conformations.
source: SBD1 (Figure 2E; Figure 4D) can sample at least four distinct ligand-bound conformations and SBD2 (Figure 2F; Figure 4E) and OpuAC (Figure 2B; Figure 4G) at least three.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and Figure 4D.

claim: SBD2 can sample at least three distinct ligand-bound conformations.
source: SBD1 (Figure 2E; Figure 4D) can sample at least four distinct ligand-bound conformations and SBD2 (Figure 2F; Figure 4E) and OpuAC (Figure 2B; Figure 4G) at least three.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F and Figure 4E.

claim: OpuAC can sample at least three distinct ligand-bound conformations.
source: SBD1 (Figure 2E; Figure 4D) can sample at least four distinct ligand-bound conformations and SBD2 (Figure 2F; Figure 4E) and OpuAC (Figure 2B; Figure 4G) at least three.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and Figure 4G.

claim: MalE, SBD1 and SBD2 have multiple distinct ligand-bound conformations that can all interact with the translocator and facilitate substrate import.
source: Moreover, MalE, SBD1 and SBD2 have multiple distinct ligand-bound conformations that can all interact with the translocator, as they all facilitate substrate import ('multiple conformations activate transport' in Figure 7; Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D-F and Figure 7.

claim: A productive SBP-translocator interaction in Type I ABC importers can be accomplished without relying on strict structural requirements for docking.
source: Thus, a productive SBP-translocator interaction in Type I ABC importers can be accomplished without relying on strict structural requirements for docking.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that multiple conformations can activate transport.

claim: This generalization may not apply to all Type I ABC importers since in the Opp importer the translocator might only interact with a unique closed conformation of the SBP OppA.
source: This generalization may not apply to all Type I ABC importers since in the Opp importer the translocator might only interact with a unique closed conformation of the SBP OppA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), and Opp has no measurable affinity for its open ligand-free conformation (Doeven et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and citation to Doeven et al., 2008.

claim: Opp has no measurable affinity for its open ligand-free conformation.
source: This generalization may not apply to all Type I ABC importers since in the Opp importer the translocator might only interact with a unique closed conformation of the SBP OppA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), and Opp has no measurable affinity for its open ligand-free conformation (Doeven et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Doeven et al., 2008.

claim: Not all SBP conformational states appear to provide the signal to facilitate transport.
source: We have shown that although multiple SBP conformations can activate transport (Figure 2D–F), not all SBP conformational states appear to provide the signal to facilitate transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some non-cognate ligands induce conformations that do not support transport.

claim: The binding of certain non-cognate ligands induces a conformational change in SBD1, MalE and OpuAC that are distinct from those that facilitate transport.
source: For example, the binding of certain non-cognate ligands induces a conformational change in SBD1 (Figure 4D), MalE (Figure 4F) and OpuAC (Figure 4G) that are distinct from those that facilitate transport.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D, 4F, and 4G.

claim: Substrate import can fail in Type I ABC importers due to the SBP-ligand complex assuming a conformation that cannot initiate allosteric interactions with the translocator.
source: These observations provide a general explanation on how substrate import can fail in Type I ABC importers, which would be due to the SBP-ligand complex assuming a conformation that cannot initiate allosteric interactions with the translocator ('conformational mismatch' in Figure 7).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The sole observation of partial closing of MalE cannot explain why transport of β-cyclodextrin fails.
source: However, the sole observation of partial closing of MalE cannot explain why transport of β-cyclodextrin fails, as we here show that also cognate maltodextrins are able to induce partial closing of MalE (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that cognate maltodextrins also induce partial closing.

claim: In PsaA, the binding site composition precludes the ability of the protein to exclude the non-cognate substrate Zn2+ from interacting.
source: In PsaA, the binding site composition of the SBP precludes the ability of the protein to exclude the non-cognate substrate Zn2+ from interacting.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both Mn2+ and Zn2+ bind to PsaA.

claim: Both Mn2+ and Zn2+ bind and trigger formation of similar PsaA conformations.
source: As a consequence, both metals bind and trigger formation of similar PsaA conformations ('conformational match' in Figure 7; Figure 4H) (McDevitt et al., 2011; Lawrence et al., 1998).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4H and supported by citations to McDevitt et al., 2011 and Lawrence et al., 1998.

claim: Zn2+ forms a highly stable closed conformation with PsaA such that it cannot open and release the substrate to its translocator.
source: Despite this, the two ions have starkly different conformational dynamics, with Zn2+ forming a highly stable closed conformation, such that it cannot open and release the substrate to its translocator ('SBP cannot open' in Figure 7; Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: By altering the binding site interactions between PsaA and Zn2+, opening is faster and transport of the metal ion can occur.
source: By altering the binding site interactions between PsaA and Zn2+, opening is faster and transport of the metal ion can occur (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: A slower/faster opening of the SBP results in a decrease/increase in the corresponding transport of the substrate or ATP hydrolysis rate for GlnPQ and MalE.
source: Similar observations were made for GlnPQ (Gouridis et al., 2015; Schuurman-Wolters et al., 2018) and MalE (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A), in which a slower/faster opening of the SBP resulted in a decrease/increase in the corresponding transport of the substrate or ATP hydrolysis rate ('faster SBP opening – faster transport' in Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gouridis et al., 2015 and Schuurman-Wolters et al., 2018, and shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: For ligands that induce highly stabilized SBP-substrate conformations, which require more energy to open, transport becomes slower or is abrogated.
source: We therefore conclude that for ligands that induce highly stabilized SBP-substrate conformations, which require more energy (thermal or ATP-dependent) to open, transport becomes slower or is abrogated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PsaA and MalE data.

claim: Biological selectivity in ABC importers is largely achieved via a combination of ligand release kinetics and its influence on the conformational state of the SBP.
source: Based on these findings, we infer that biological selectivity in ABC importers is largely achieved via a combination of ligand release kinetics and its influence on the conformational state of the SBP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The translocator contributes to the specificity of ABC importers.
source: However, our data also implicate a role for the translocator in contributing to the specificity of ABC importers ('rejected by translocator' in Figure 7), consistent with previous studies (Oldham et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2015; Davidson et al., 1992; Speiser and Ames, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The presence of a substrate binding site in the translocator of the maltose system is well-established.
source: The presence of a substrate binding site in the translocator of the maltose system is well-established (Oldham et al., 2013), although its role, if any, in influencing the rate of transport of maltodextrins is yet unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oldham et al., 2013.

claim: The role of the substrate binding site in the translocator in influencing the rate of transport of maltodextrins is yet unknown.
source: The presence of a substrate binding site in the translocator of the maltose system is well-established (Oldham et al., 2013), although its role, if any, in influencing the rate of transport of maltodextrins is yet unknown.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: The positive correlation between lifetime of the SBP closed state and activity of the transporter implies that some maltodextrins trigger certain steps more efficiently than other maltodextrins.
source: Irrespective of the precise molecular mechanism, the positive correlation between lifetime of the SBP closed state and activity of the transporter implies that some maltodextrins trigger certain steps more efficient than other maltodextrins, thereby overcoming the slower opening of MalE, and leading to a preferred uptake of certain maltodextrins over others.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis in Figure 6H.

claim: Some maltodextrins trigger certain steps more efficiently than others, leading to a preferred uptake of certain maltodextrins over others.
source: Irrespective of the precise molecular mechanism, the positive correlation between lifetime of the SBP closed state and activity of the transporter implies that some maltodextrins trigger certain steps more efficient than other maltodextrins, thereby overcoming the slower opening of MalE, and leading to a preferred uptake of certain maltodextrins over others.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the correlation analysis.

claim: When transport is solely altered by changing the SBP conformational dynamics, the kinetics of downstream steps are not affected.
source: When transport is solely altered by changing the SBP conformational dynamics, for example in MalE(I329W/A96W) and PsaA(D280N), the kinetics of these steps are not affected, as the same ligands are involved, thus explaining the negative correlation between SBP lifetime and transport in these specific cases.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant studies.

claim: The volume of the binding cavities in the translocator could be a limiting factor for transport via ABC importers.
source: The volume of the binding cavities in the translocator could be a limiting factor for transport via ABC importers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the maltooctaose/maltodecaose data.

claim: Failure of the maltose system to transport maltooctaose and maltodecaose most likely arises due to size limitations of the translocator rather than failure of MalE to close and release the bound ligand.
source: Therefore, failure of the maltose system to transport maltooctaose and maltodecaose most likely arises due to size limitations of the translocator rather than failure of MalE to close and release the bound ligand.
evidence: This is concluded from the similar opening kinetics for maltoheptaose, maltooctaose, and maltodecaose.

claim: Analysis of the binding cavities in the crystal structure of MalFGK2-MalE suggests that the transporter could only accommodate maltodextrins as large as maltoheptaose.
source: This supposition is supported by an analysis of the binding cavities in the crystal structure of MalFGK2-MalE (Oldham et al., 2013). These data suggest that the transporter could only accommodate maltodextrins as large as maltoheptoase.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oldham et al., 2013.

claim: MalE could accommodate larger maltodextrins, including β-cyclodextrin, probably due to its greater structural flexibility.
source: In contrast, MalE could accommodate larger maltodextrins, including β-cyclodextrin (Figure 4F), probably due to its greater structural flexibility (Figure 2D; Figure 4F), thereby allowing the binding pocket to adapt and ligands to extend into the solvent phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing binding of large maltodextrins.

claim: The presence of two consecutive binding pockets, one in the SBP and one in the translocator, in at least some ABC importers could indicate that specificity of transport occurs through a proofreading mechanism.
source: The presence of two consecutive binding pockets, one in the SBP and one in the translocator, in at least some ABC importers could indicate that specificity of transport occurs through a proofreading mechanism in a manner analogous to aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and DNA polymerase (Shevelev and Hübscher, 2002; Kotik-Kogan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to proofreading mechanisms in other systems.

claim: In a proofreading mechanism, a substrate can be rejected even if it has been bound by the SBP.
source: In such a mechanism, a substrate can be rejected even if it has been bound by the SBP.
evidence: This is a description of how a proofreading mechanism would work.

claim: Intrinsic closing is a rare event in SBPs.
source: Although we show that intrinsic closing is a rare event ('little intrinsic closing' in Figure 7; data in Figure 3), it might influence transport in a cellular context where the ratio between SBP and translocator can be high (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Figure 7.

claim: Intrinsic closing might influence transport in a cellular context where the ratio between SBP and translocator can be high.
source: Although we show that intrinsic closing is a rare event ('little intrinsic closing' in Figure 7; data in Figure 3), it might influence transport in a cellular context where the ratio between SBP and translocator can be high (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2016.

claim: Other fast (µs-ms) and short-range conformational changes might be present in SBPs as shown by NMR analysis on MalE.
source: Moreover, other fast (µs-ms) and short-range conformational changes might be present as shown by NMR analysis on MalE (Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2007.

claim: In Type I ABC importers, the wasteful conversion of chemical energy is prevented by a proofreading mechanism.
source: We speculate that in Type I ABC importers the wasteful conversion of chemical energy is prevented by a proofreading mechanism, as any thermally driven closing event would not be able to initiate the translocation cycle, as the substrate is absent.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of intrinsic closing.

claim: Any thermally driven closing event would not be able to initiate the translocation cycle, as the substrate is absent.
source: We speculate that in Type I ABC importers the wasteful conversion of chemical energy is prevented by a proofreading mechanism, as any thermally driven closing event would not be able to initiate the translocation cycle, as the substrate is absent.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the proofreading hypothesis.

claim: ATP hydrolysis and transport are tightly coupled in the Type I importer GlnPQ.
source: In accordance, ATP hydrolysis and transport are tightly coupled in the Type I importer GlnPQ (Lycklama A Nijeholt et al., 2018) that, based on the crystal structure of the homologous Art(QM)2 (Yu et al., 2015), contains an internal binding pocket located within the TMDs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lycklama A Nijeholt et al., 2018.

claim: GlnPQ contains an internal binding pocket located within the TMDs based on the crystal structure of the homologous Art(QM)2.
source: In accordance, ATP hydrolysis and transport are tightly coupled in the Type I importer GlnPQ (Lycklama A Nijeholt et al., 2018) that, based on the crystal structure of the homologous Art(QM)2 (Yu et al., 2015), contains an internal binding pocket located within the TMDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure of Art(QM)2 cited (Yu et al., 2015).

claim: Futile hydrolysis of ATP in the Type II importer BtuCDF appears to correlate with the lack of a defined binding pocket inside the TMDs.
source: By contrast, futile hydrolysis of ATP in the Type II importer BtuCDF (Borths et al., 2005) appears to correlate with the lack of a defined binding pocket inside the TMDs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borths et al., 2005.
